About me

I’m Alejandro Hennessey, a Toronto-based product designer working across UX, e-commerce, visual systems, and motion. I turn messy product questions into clear flows, confident interfaces, and systems teams can actually ship.

I’m drawn to the space between a complicated idea and the moment it finally makes sense. My work sits between product thinking, visual craft, and business reality: I have designed and operated real storefronts, shaped product concepts, collaborated with developers, and built visual systems that make an experience feel coherent from first touch to delivery.

I care about making design useful, not just polished — clear enough for people to trust and considered enough for teams to build on.

What I work across

  • UI/UX design — user research, information architecture, user flows, wireframing, prototyping, and usability testing
  • Graphic design — branding, typography, illustration, editorial design, and motion graphics
  • E-commerce — Shopify storefronts, catalogues, promotional campaigns, and conversion-focused strategy

The person behind the work

Curious by nature.
Practical by design.

I’m a designer who likes asking better questions before making more screens. I want to understand what people are trying to do, what is getting in their way, and what the business needs the experience to achieve. That balance keeps my work grounded: expressive enough to be memorable, structured enough to be useful.

My background in graphic design gives me a strong eye for hierarchy, typography, colour, and composition. My product work has taught me to think in systems, flows, constraints, and real decisions. Together, they help me move comfortably from the first sketch to a polished interface and the details that make it feel finished.

“The best interface is not the one that shows the most work. It is the one that makes the next decision feel obvious.”

KitLab FS

Technical Specs
Role
UX/UI Designer & E-commerce Manager
Timeline
8 weeks, audit → handoff
Format
Shopify storefront (desktop & mobile)
Screens
42 high-fidelity screens
Overview

KitLab FS offers thousands of club, national-team, and retro football jerseys. I redesigned the storefront to simplify product discovery, clarify customization options, and create a smoother shopping experience across desktop and mobile.

The Problem

The original shopping experience made it difficult to navigate a large catalogue and understand options like player versions, patches, sizing, and name customization.

How might we help customers move from browsing thousands of jerseys to a confident purchase — without the interface feeling overloaded at any step?

The Approach

I reorganized the information architecture, improved collection filtering, and redesigned the product page to help customers find the right jersey and purchase it with greater confidence. My priority wasn't adding more features — it was making each decision easier to understand.

Designed for discovery

Products are organized around how customers naturally search — by club, country, competition, season, and jersey type — with filters progressively revealed to avoid overload.

Built for confidence

Version, size, name, number, and patches follow a guided sequence. The interface updates selection and price live as customers build their jersey.

Scalable by design

Reusable, flexible product cards and consistent interface patterns let KitLab FS expand its catalogue while keeping the experience cohesive.

Figma artifacts / 01

The flow works as a sequence

A closer look at the screens that shaped the redesign: product confidence first, then the mobile discovery rhythm, then the cart moment where intent becomes commitment.

MatchUp

Mobile app (iOS / Android)
Users
Organizers & players
Overview

A mobile platform for creating local soccer matches, selecting available positions, and sharing the field-booking cost between players. MatchUp connects organizers who've already booked a field with players looking for local games — who can review the match, inspect both teams, and choose an open position before joining.

I designed the connected player and organizer experiences: match discovery, team formation, position selection, cost sharing, match management, player rankings, and post-match reviews.

The Problem

Players rely on scattered group chats and social posts to find games, with incomplete information on cost, skill level, and open positions. Organizers pay for fields upfront, manually build teams, and repeatedly chase payments.

How might we turn an informal, unreliable group-chat process into a trusted experience for forming teams, selecting positions, and sharing field costs — for two very different users at once?

Two core users, one system

The experience had to coordinate two different journeys while keeping team availability, player ability, and field costs understandable at every stage.

Field booked → match ready

A single mapped flow — setup, publish, discover, select, confirm — keeps organizer and player actions in sync from booking through kickoff.

Transparent cost sharing

Costs are calculated and split automatically across paid positions, replacing manual chasing with a clear, shared total.

Figma artifacts / 02

Designing toward kickoff

The MatchUp story is a chain of trust: discover a real game, inspect the context on a map, then return after the match with a shared record of what happened.

01 / 03Discover games

Decision trail / 02

From coordination to kickoff

MatchUp needed to feel social without becoming chaotic. I treated organizer and player actions as connected states in one flow, so trust could build before the match started.

CommerceFlow

Technical Specs
Role

Type

Modules

Users
Multi-store operators
Overview

A centralized SaaS platform for monitoring performance, managing operations, and comparing multiple e-commerce stores. CommerceFlow brings sales, orders, inventory, customers, and advertising data into one connected workspace — helping multi-store operators spot urgent issues and act, without switching between dashboards and spreadsheets.

The Problem

Multi-store operators repeatedly switch between storefronts, advertising platforms, spreadsheets, and supplier systems just to understand performance and manage daily operations.

My approach: I organized the platform around the decisions users make each day rather than the tools where the data originated. The overview communicates what changed; each module explains why. Critical issues surface as actionable alerts linked directly to the screen where they're resolved.

Designed around decisions

Not data sources. Every module answers a question an operator actually asks each morning.

Alerts that lead somewhere

Each flagged issue connects straight to the screen where it can be investigated and resolved — no hunting required.

Built to scale

A component system that supports growing catalogues, additional stores, and different team roles without fragmenting the experience.

Decision trail / 03

From data sprawl to a decision surface

CommerceFlow becomes useful when an operator can scan what changed, understand why, and move directly into the right action. The hierarchy is designed around that rhythm.

Motion study / 03Signal → action
COMMERCE / 03
A moving overview of the decisions-first workspace.
Signal

Context was expensive

Operators had to assemble a story from multiple systems before they could act.

Design bet

Overview first, detail second

Make change legible at a glance, then use modules to explain and resolve it.

Proof

A calmer operating loop

When alerts lead somewhere useful, a dense dashboard becomes a decision tool instead of another inbox.
